newsitem.title: FRANCE: France heaps praise on Clinton, dispute looms.
newsitem.headline: France heaps praise on Clinton, dispute looms.

text.p: France heaped praise on re-elected U.S. President Bill Clinton on Wednesday, President Jacques Chirac effusively pledging closer cooperation with an old ally with whom ties have often been prickly.
Analysts said, however, that Chirac's unusually warm message was aimed primarily at his domestic audience and that Washington and Paris would remain at odds on many global matters in coming years.

A dispute was already looming as Washington showed little enthusiasm for a French proposal to send a multinational force including U.S. troops to help get food to one million starving refugees caught in fighting in Zaire.
"I have just heard the joyful news...may I say that no one is more delighted than I am," Chirac wrote to Clinton.

"Your presence at the White House will guarantee us an American partner who is friendly, clear-sighted, competent, but also generous. I know that with your re-election the close relations between our two countries will become even closer."
Foreign Minister Herve de Charette, in a television interview, called Clinton "packed with talent, cultured, very intelligent, very open, clever, skilful, a man with a real dimension".
Chirac, who like Clinton is likely to rule into the next century, added a personal telephone call to his written message.
His office said both voiced "conviction that their countries would keep cooperating in a spirit of shared friendship to lead their countries into the 21st century".
Commentators agreed his note was the warmest -- and the only one written in English -- to be made public by the Elysee presidential palace since Chirac moved in 18 months ago.
In another first, the Elysee released an equally warm message to Hillary Clinton from Chirac's wife.

"Jacques and I are really deeply happy at the thought that we shall be seeing you regularly in the coming years," Bernadette Chirac wrote. The four dined together at an upmarket Paris restaurant during the June summit of the Group of Seven industrial powers in Lyon.

"Chirac wants to show he has a warm and close personal relationship with Clinton, but a personal relationship is not the same thing as foreign policy," said Pascal Boniface, head of France's Institute for International and Strategic Relations.

"There have been numerous major policy differences in the recent past, and there will be more confrontations in the future," said Boniface, who nonetheless joked that Chirac's note sounded like "a declaration of love".
Opinion polls in France had shown that Clinton was overwhelmingly favoured by French citizens over Dole.
But they also found the French increasingly disenchanted with the United States, believing it to be too influential in the world and scarred by violence.
French officials, who have expressed irritation in recent months at U.S. policy in the Middle East and Africa, predicted few changes in U.S. policy goals abroad.
De Charette, who once said Paris "irritated" Washington in the Middle East, told France-Inter radio he thought Clinton would turn more towards foreign policy in his second term.
Ex-president Valery Giscard d'Estaing, who ruled from 1974 to 1981, predicted that Washington would become more self-assured abroad and increasingly unwilling to share responsibility with its allies.
In international policy "they want to act all alone, they want to solve the problems of the Middle East, they don't accept intervention by others," Giscard d'Estaing told RTL radio.
